messages.author: 9d61e7b0823c1527
messages.subject: constraining one vector of a 2-d array or matrix
parts:
I would like to constrain one vector of a matrix or 2-d array to be positive, but leave the other vector unconstrained.

This is for a factor analysis model that is parameterized as a hierarchical linear model (i.e., like an IRT model, with manifest variables stacked in "long" format). In particular, I would like to constrain the factor loadings / slopes to be positive to deal with reflection invariance, but let the intercepts be positive or negative. 

I also want the intercepts and slopes to be bound as a matrix (or 2-d array) so I can model their correlation using the code from pg 54 of the current stan manual. Looking at that code, the matrix in question is beta.

Any idea how I might go about doing this?

the matrix for linear algebra manipulations then you can construct the
two arrays and then concatenate them into a matrix in transformed
parameters (or locally to the model block).  Right now I believe this has
to be done with a loop as many of the matrix slide/dice operations are
still in development.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] constraining one vector of a 2-d array or matrix
parts:
On Thursday, November 27, 2014 10:17:59 AM UTC-5, Christopher Claassen wrote:
Thanks Michael. I think I have tried something like that -- the relevant lines of my model are below, with Beta being the matrix in question.

There is now an append_col() function that can take two vectors and combine them into a two-column matrix, which would slightly simplify your transformed parameters block. But the deeper problem is with the model block:

model{  
  alpha ~ normal(0, 1);
  beta ~ normal(0, 1);
       
  for (j in 1:J)  
    Beta[j] ~ multi_normal(mu_Beta, Sigma_Beta);
}

First, if you are going to put a prior on alpha and beta, then it does not make sense to put a prior on Beta, which is just alpha and beta together.

Second, if beta is constrained to be strictly positive, then a normal prior is inappropriate because it spreads its unit of mass over the whole real line.

One option would be to specify a normal prior on alpha, and then a truncated normal prior on beta conditional on alpha.

From Wikipedia, the untruncated conditional distribution of beta (X_1) given alpha (X_2) is


Then, if the prior means are both 0 and the prior standard deviations are both 1, you would just need to write that in Stan code

conditional_sd <- sqrt(1 - square(rho))
for(j in 1:J) {
  beta[j] ~ normal(rho * alpha[j], conditional_sd) T[0,];
}

Ben

> On Nov 27, 2014, at 11:37 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

I'm confused. I don't see what's wrong with writing

parameters {
matrix<lower=0>[M,N] alpha;
vector[M] beta;
...

model {
matrix[M, N + 1] gamma;
...
gamma <- append_col(alpha,beta);
gamma ~ normal(0,1);
...


It'll put a half normal prior on the elements of alpha
and a normal prior on beta.

Now it may not be a good modeling idea, but that's a separate
issue.

And it won't work if the constraints on alpha depend on beta,
but here they don't.

- Bob

parts: On Thursday, November 27, 2014 1:32:33 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> On Nov 27, 2014, at 11:37 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>
> ...

> First, if you are going to put a prior on alpha and beta, then it does not make sense to put a prior on Beta, which is just alpha and beta together.
>
> Second, if beta is constrained to be strictly positive, then a normal prior is inappropriate because it spreads its unit of mass over the whole real line.

It'll put a half normal prior on the elements of alpha
and a normal prior on beta.

Now it may not be a good modeling idea, but that's a separate
issue.

And it won't work if the constraints on alpha depend on beta,
but here they don't.
It depends on what Christopher intended when he miswrote this "double prior" thing

model{  
  alpha ~ normal(0, 1);
  beta ~ normal(0, 1);
       
  for (j in 1:J)  
    Beta[j] ~ multi_normal(mu_Beta, Sigma_Beta);
}

If you get rid of the multi_normal() statement, then Bob's normal and half-normal prior remains. If you get rid of the two normal() statements, then you get a wrong, untruncated prior. Multivariate normal priors are typical in this literature, so that is what I was assuming he really meant. Stan doesn't have a truncated multivariate normal distribution, but if only one dimension is inequality constrained, then you can get by with a (possibly multivariate) normal on the unconstrained dimension(s) and a univariate truncated conditional normal distribution on the constrained dimension.

Ben

messages.author: 9d61e7b0823c1527
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] constraining one vector of a 2-d array or matrix
parts: Thank everyone for all the replies. I think I need this prior for Beta

for (j in 1:J)  
    Beta[j] ~ multi_normal(mu_Beta, Sigma_Beta);

because I want to model the correlation, which is in Sigma_Beta. But this unconstrained prior leads to the slopes / factor loadings jumping between +ve and -ve across chains as Ben notes.

However, based on advice supplied in section 18.2 in the manual, I used an unconstrained matrix of parameters, a positive set of initial values for the vector of slopes, and only one chain. This works nicely.

My full program is very similar to the hierarchical linear model on pg 54 of the manual, although without group-level predictors and with a vector of factor scores to be estimated instead of a set of individual level predictors.


data{
  int<lower=1> N;               // number of individuals
int<lower=1> J;               // number of raters

int<lower=1> K;               // number of ratings
  int<lower=1,upper=N> ii[K];   // individual for rating k
  int<lower=1,upper=J> jj[K];   // rater for rating k
  real x[K];                    // ratings
  vector<lower=1>[N] eta_1;     // vector of 1s
}
parameters{
  vector[N] eta;                // factor scores
  real<lower=0> sigma_x;        // variance of residuals
  corr_matrix[2] Omega;  
  vector<lower=0>[2] tau;
  vector[2] Beta[J];            // matrix of parameters
  vector[2] mu_beta;
}
transformed parameters{
  matrix[N,2] Eta;
  Eta <- append_col(eta_1, eta);
}
model{
  matrix[2,2] Sigma_Beta;
  Sigma_Beta <- quad_form_diag(Omega, tau);

  sigma_x ~ uniform(0, 100);
  eta ~ normal(0, 1);           // identify scale and location  
  mu_beta ~ normal(0, 1);
  tau ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  Omega ~ lkj_corr(2);

  Beta ~ multi_normal(mu_beta, Sigma_Beta);

  for (k in 1:K)  
    x[k] ~ normal(Eta[ii[k]] * Beta[jj[k]], sigma_x);
}

with indexing. Writing

mu_Beta ~ normal(0,1);

is just a more efficient (memory and run time) way of writing:

for (j in 1:2)
